title: Every file upload returns HTTP 500 in the launch configuration (bigint overflow from the unlimited-plan sentinel)
what: When subscriptions are off, EffectivePlanService.unlimitedPlan() rewrites every int feature to UNLIMITED_INT = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991). StorageService.put then computes `const limitBytes = BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n` = 9444732965739289378816 and interpolates it into the atomic reservation `UPDATE tenants SET "storageUsedBytes" = ... WHERE "storageUsedBytes" + $n <= ${limitBytes}`. That literal exceeds Postgres bigint (max 9223372036854775807), so the statement fails with SQLSTATE 22003 before any file is written. Every upload path funnels through StorageService.put: book covers (catalog/covers.controller.ts), member photos (members/photos.controller.ts), library logos (branding/branding.controller.ts) and the generic storage endpoint. Note the switch is the platform_settings row `billing.enabled`, which is seeded to 'false' and OVERRIDES the BILLING_ENABLED env var (platform-settings.service.ts:39), so setting the env var true does not avoid it.
impact: On launch day, with subscriptions disabled as planned, no library can upload a single book cover, member photo, or their own logo. Every attempt returns the generic 'something went wrong, here is a support code' 500. This is the first thing a librarian does after adding a book. It is not degraded behaviour, it is total failure of the whole upload feature, and it will read to the customer as 'the product is broken'.
evidence: EXECUTED against the live audit env. `POST /t/probes1-x9/storage/covers` with a 7-byte image/png returned 500. API log: `Invalid prisma.$executeRaw() invocation: Raw query failed. Code: 22003. Message: value "9444732965739289378816" is out of range for type bigint ... at async StorageService.put (apps/api/src/storage/storage.service.ts:76)`. Confirmed the arithmetic: 9007199254740991 x 1048576 = 9444732965739289378816 exactly. Confirmed the source: `GET /t/probes1-x9/plan` returns `max_storage_mb = {"type":"int","value":9007199254740991,"source":"override","note":"Included - subscriptions are currently disabled."}`. Confirmed the gate: `select key,value from platform_settings` -> `billing.enabled|false`. A cover upload succeeded (201, ref covers/cmt5mnc442df6cc8c2af8.png) only during a window where the settings cache still held billing=true; once the cache re-read the DB row every upload 500s again, including a 12 MB one.
fix: Clamp the byte ceiling before it reaches SQL. In StorageService.put: `const limitBytes = limitMb >= Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER ? 9223372036854775807n : BigInt(limitMb) * 1024n * 1024n;` — or better, skip the conditional UPDATE entirely and do an unconditional increment when the plan is unlimited. Add an integration test that runs the upload path with `billing.enabled=false`; the existing suite only exercises it with a real plan, which is why this was never caught.

title: Every rate limit and the account lockout key off a client-supplied header, so all of them are bypassed by rotating X-Real-IP
what: clientIp() reads `X-Real-IP` from the request with no check on who sent it. Everything that throttles unauthenticated abuse is keyed on that value: the per-IP signup cap (5/10min), the per-IP login cap (20/5min), the per-IP password-reset cap, the /apply form cap (5/hour) and — critically — the brute-force lockout itself, which login.service.ts:15 keys as `login:fail:<uid>:<ip>` and `login:lock:<uid>:<ip>` (comment A1-01). Changing one header per request gives every request a fresh, empty bucket. The code justifies trusting the header with a comment (client-ip.ts:9, repeated in infra/caddy/Caddyfile:175): 'The host firewall only admits Cloudflare's ranges, so the header cannot be spoofed by hitting the origin directly.' No such firewall exists anywhere in the repo. There is no ufw/iptables/nftables rule in scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh, scripts/deploy-on-host.sh, infra/compose/* or infra/deploy/fleet.yml, and the one documented procedure the operator will follow (docs/deployment-hetzner.md:192-199) is `ufw allow 80/tcp` / `ufw allow 443/tcp` — open to the entire internet, not Cloudflare ranges. Caddy then does `header_up X-Real-IP {http.request.header.CF-Connecting-IP}`, so an attacker hitting the origin IP directly with a forged CF-Connecting-IP has Caddy stamp the forgery into X-Real-IP for them. The origin IP (195.201.13.95) is in the repo.
impact: There is no working defence against password guessing, signup flooding, or form spam. An attacker can (a) brute-force any known account without ever tripping the lockout, (b) provision unlimited tenant Postgres databases through /auth/signup, and (c) flood the marketing form. All audit-log IP attribution is also attacker-controlled: an intruder chooses what IP appears next to their actions in the audit trail.
evidence: EXECUTED against the live audit env. (1) Login limiter: 25 POSTs to /auth/login with a fixed `X-Real-IP: 9.9.9.9` -> 20x401 then 5x429, limiter works. The same 25 with `X-Real-IP: 10.0.0.$i` -> 25x401, zero 429. (2) Account lockout: 40 wrong-password POSTs against the real account owner@libwf-be65e9.test with a rotating X-Real-IP -> 40x401, no 429, and `select failedLogins, lockedUntil from users` shows failedLogins=40 with lockedUntil NULL — the lockout never fired once. (3) /apply: 8 submissions from one IP -> 5x303 then 3x429; 8 with rotating IPs -> 8x303, all persisted (applications table went to 13 rows). (4) READ: grep for ufw|iptables|nftables|firewall across scripts/, infra/ returns no rule anywhere; docs/deployment-hetzner.md:196-197 is `ufw allow 80/tcp` + `ufw allow 443/tcp`.
fix: Two changes, both needed. (a) Stop trusting the header unconditionally: in client-ip.ts, only honour X-Real-IP when the TCP peer (`req.socket.remoteAddress`) is in an allowlist of trusted proxy addresses (the Caddy container IP / a TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS env var); otherwise fall back to req.socket.remoteAddress. (b) Make the deploy actually implement the assumption the code documents: add the Cloudflare-range-restricted 80/443 rules to scripts/prod-bootstrap.sh (pull https://www.cloudflare.com/ips-v4 and -v6) so the control is code, not a sentence in a markdown file, and fix docs/deployment-hetzner.md:196-197 which currently tells the operator to do the opposite. Additionally, give the account lockout a bare-account component with a much higher threshold on top of the per-(account+IP) one, so IP rotation cannot make it unreachable.

title: Unauthenticated signup provisions a Postgres database per request with no admission control that an attacker cannot bypass
what: POST /auth/signup is unauthenticated and each success runs TenantProvisioningService: CREATE DATABASE plus a full Prisma migration fork, ~1.1s of server work and a permanent Postgres database. The only hard gate is the per-IP bucket `signup:ip:<ip>` (5/10min), which is keyed on the spoofable header from finding 02. The global bucket `signup:global` is deliberately advisory — alarmIfOverBudget() (auth.controller.ts:107-119) logs and returns, it never rejects. So after the IP key is defeated there is literally nothing left that refuses a signup. There is no CAPTCHA, no email-verification-before-provisioning, and no queue depth limit.
impact: One host can create tenant databases as fast as the box can fork migrations. Each one is a permanent Postgres database on the same cluster as every paying library, consuming connection slots, disk, backup time and the nightly DR window. This is the 'unauth signup DoS' critical the 2026-06 audit recorded; the remediation added a per-IP limiter, which the header spoof removes. The advisory-only global cap means the system has no backstop by design.
evidence: EXECUTED. 8 signups from a fixed `X-Real-IP: 7.7.7.7` -> 5x201 then 3x429 (the cap works). 8 signups with `X-Real-IP: 7.7.8.$i` -> 8x201, all provisioned. API log shows `Created tenant database tenant_cmt5mjvf2d566...` etc. for each. Tenants table went from 3 to 17 rows over the run; each request took ~1.15s of server time. READ: auth.controller.ts:107-119 `alarmIfOverBudget` only calls `this.logger.error(...)` and never throws.
fix: Fix the IP source per finding 02, then add an admission control that does not depend on the client's identity claim: provision the tenant database only after the owner clicks the email verification link (create the control-plane row immediately, defer CREATE DATABASE), and/or put a Turnstile/hCaptcha check in front of the form. Additionally cap the number of tenants in 'provisioning' state globally and reject (not just log) past that.

title: The help-article HTML sanitizer is a regex denylist with proven bypasses, feeding dangerouslySetInnerHTML under a CSP that allows inline script
what: renderHtml() runs `marked` (which passes raw HTML straight through) then sanitizeHtml(), four `.replace()` calls that strip active-content tags, `on*=` handlers, and `href|src="javascript:`. The scheme regex requires a quote immediately after `=`, so an unquoted attribute slips past; it matches the literal string `javascript:`, so an HTML-entity-encoded scheme slips past; and it only looks at href/src, so SVG's `<animate attributeName=href values=javascript:...>` slips past. The stored bodyHtml is then injected with dangerouslySetInnerHTML inside the authenticated tenant shell. The CSP set at apps/web/next.config.mjs:57 is `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, which permits javascript: URL execution, so there is no containment layer behind the sanitizer. The file's own comment claims the function exists as 'defense-in-depth so a future content edit (or an admin-authored-help feature) can't introduce stored XSS' — that claim is false.
impact: Today the only author is someone with commit access, so this is not remotely exploitable — the harm is that the guard the team believes they have does not hold. The moment help content becomes admin-authored (the comment anticipates exactly that), or a markdown file is added via a dependency/vendor/AI-assisted edit that nobody reads as HTML, it becomes stored XSS in the tenant shell against every librarian in every library, with a CSP that will not stop it.
evidence:
EXECUTED. Ran marked@18.0.10 + a verbatim copy of sanitizeHtml over 12 payloads. Survivors: `x` -> output `

x

` (unquoted attribute, regex needs a quote); `[click](javascript:alert(1))` -> ``; `` -> passed through verbatim; `
fix: Replace sanitizeHtml() with an allowlist sanitizer — `sanitize-html` or `isomorphic-dompurify` — configured with an explicit allowed tag/attribute set and `allowedSchemes: ['http','https','mailto']`. The dependency is already justified by the comment in the file. Do it before any admin-authored help feature ships, not after.

title: A NUL byte in any text query parameter produces an HTTP 500, including on the unauthenticated /help/articles endpoint
what: Query strings are passed to Prisma/Postgres without stripping U+0000. Postgres rejects a NUL in a text value with SQLSTATE 22021 ('invalid byte sequence for encoding UTF8: 0x00'), Prisma throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError, and HttpExceptionFilter turns it into a 500 with a support code. No DTO validation runs on query parameters at all — validateDto is only applied to request bodies (main.ts:47 documents that there is no global ValidationPipe), and the query helpers in platform/query.ts only cover numeric params.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can generate 500s at will against /help/articles?q=%00 — every one writes a full error record with a stack trace to the logs and mints a support code. That is a cheap log-flood / alert-fatigue lever on a public endpoint, and it will pollute whatever error budget or paging the team wires up. For signed-in users it is a plain robustness defect: a paste containing a stray NUL turns a search box into 'something went wrong'.
evidence: EXECUTED. All returned 500: `GET /help/articles?q=%00` with NO cookie (unauthenticated), `GET /t/probes1-x9/members?q=%00`, `.../catalog/books?q=%00`, `.../catalog/authors?q=%00`, `.../audit?after=%00`. The same endpoints with normal input return 200. API log for the audit case: `Invalid prisma.auditEvent.findMany() invocation: Database error. Code: 22021. Message: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00 ... at async AuditService.list`.
fix: Add a tiny middleware (or extend platform/query.ts with a `parseText(raw)` helper used by every string @Query) that strips control characters including U+0000 from query values before they reach a service. Strip, don't reject — a NUL is never meaningful search input.

title: Import staging writes 64 MB files to the shared storage volume with no quota, no batch cap and no cleanup sweeper
what: createBatch() stages the raw upload at STORAGE_ROOT/_imports/<batchId>.<ext>, up to IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES = 64 MB per file. The file is deliberately excluded from the tenant's max_storage_mb quota (documented in the module header: 'Staged here rather than in tenant storage so the file does NOT count against the tenant's max_storage_mb quota'). Nothing else bounds it: there is no cap on how many batches a tenant may leave in 'uploaded' status, and the file is only removed by remove()/finish. Exports have a cleanup sweeper (apps/api/src/jobs/export-cleanup.job.ts); imports have none — grep across apps/api/src/jobs and apps/api/src/maintenance finds no reference to _imports, stagingPath or deleteStaged.
impact: Any tenant owner/admin (or one compromised admin account, or an honest librarian retrying a failing import twenty times) can fill the shared storage volume 64 MB at a time and never trigger a limit. That volume also holds every other tenant's covers and photos and is where export artifacts are written, so exhausting it breaks uploads, exports and the backup job for every library on the box at once. Abandoned batches accumulate indefinitely even without malice.
evidence: READ. import.constants.ts:7 `IMPORT_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES = 64 * 1024 * 1024`. import-staging.ts:9-10 module header states the quota exclusion explicitly. import.service.ts createBatch() calls `stageFile(batch.id, ..., input.file.buffer)` with no preceding count/size check of existing batches. `grep -rn 'importBatch|_imports|stagingPath|deleteStaged|sweep' apps/api/src/jobs apps/api/src/maintenance` returns only export/announcement/fine/reservation sweepers — no import sweeper exists.
fix: Two lines of defence: (a) in createBatch, refuse when the tenant already has N batches in status 'uploaded'/'mapped' (N=3 is generous) or when the sum of their sizeBytes exceeds a per-tenant staging budget; (b) add a sweeper alongside sweepExpiredExports that deletes staged files and rows for batches left un-run for more than ~24h.

title: Deeply nested JSON on unauthenticated endpoints blows the stack inside class-transformer and returns 500
what: validateDto passes the raw parsed body to class-transformer's plainToInstance before any structural check. class-transformer walks the object recursively with no depth bound, so a body like `{"a":{"a":{...}}}` nested ~5000 deep — well under the 100 KB body cap, so it is accepted by the parser — overflows the V8 stack with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` inside TransformOperationExecutor.getKeys. Reachable unauthenticated on /auth/login and /auth/signup, and on every authenticated write.
impact: A 40 KB request from anyone on the internet produces a 500 plus a full RangeError stack trace in the logs. Cheap unauthenticated error-log flooding, same alert-fatigue problem as finding 05. It is contained today because the throw happens synchronously inside an async handler and Nest catches it — but main.ts:74-80 installs `process.on('uncaughtException', ... process.exit(1))`, so any future refactor that moves this work outside a caught async boundary turns the same request into a process kill.
evidence: EXECUTED. Depth 5000: `POST /auth/login` (no auth) -> 500, `POST /auth/signup` (no auth) -> 500. Depth 2000 -> 400 (validation, fine). Depth 20000/60000 -> 413 (body cap). API log: `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded at TransformOperationExecutor.getKeys (class-transformer@0.5.1/src/TransformOperationExecutor.ts:527:17)`. Server stayed up (healthz 200) throughout.
fix: Add a depth guard at the top of validateDto: walk the raw value iteratively and throw BadRequestException past a modest depth (8 is more than any DTO here needs) before plainToInstance ever sees it. Same helper protects every controller at once.

title: Stored content type is discarded on download; every cover, photo and logo is served as application/octet-stream with nosniff
what: The download handlers take the Content-Type from `stat()`, but StatResult.contentType is optional (drivers/storage-driver.ts:45) and LocalDriver.stat() (drivers/local-driver.ts:78-88) never populates it — it returns only ref, sizeBytes and lastModified. The validated MIME type accepted at upload time is written nowhere: StorageService.put returns it to the caller but nothing persists it, and the on-disk filename extension is not consulted on read. sendFile therefore always falls back to `application/octet-stream`, and pairs it with `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
impact: Every image in the product is served with a wrong content type. The web UI renders covers with `` (apps/web/app/[locale]/t/[slug]/catalog/[id]/CoverUploader.tsx:96); whether a browser will paint an image declared application/octet-stream under nosniff is version- and engine-dependent rather than guaranteed, so this is a live risk of blank cover/photo/logo tiles across the app. Independently, anything that downloads these files gets a generic binary with no type information.
evidence: EXECUTED. Uploaded an image/png then fetched it back: response headers were `content-type: application/octet-stream`, `content-disposition: attachment; filename="cmt5mnlskf8250764cdd8.png"`, `x-content-type-options: nosniff`. READ: local-driver.ts stat() returns `{ ref, sizeBytes: s.size, lastModified: s.mtime }` with no contentType; storage-driver.ts:45 marks the field optional.
fix: Derive the type from the stored extension on read (a small extension->MIME map, the inverse of pickExtension) and return it from LocalDriver.stat, or persist the validated contentType alongside the ref. Verify a cover actually renders in Chrome and Safari afterwards.

title: Uploads trust the client's Content-Type entirely; no magic-byte check and no multer fileFilter
where: apps/api/src/storage/storage.service.ts:56 (ALLOWED_TYPES check against input.contentType), callers at catalog/covers.controller.ts:41, members/photos.controller.ts:40, branding/branding.controller.ts:57
what: The MIME allowlist is applied to `file.mimetype`, which is whatever the client typed in the multipart part header. The file bytes are never sniffed, and FileInterceptor is configured with `limits: { fileSize }` only — no fileFilter. So arbitrary content can be stored under an image resource type by lying about the Content-Type. The team is aware: allowed-types.ts:4 says 'Clients can lie about Content-Type, so we ALSO serve uploaded files with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff'.
impact: Low as shipped — the attachment + nosniff pairing does neutralise the 'HTML uploaded as JPEG' rendering attack, and the storage layer names files itself so the extension cannot be attacker-chosen. The residual is that tenant storage will accumulate files whose type is a lie, which matters if a future feature ever serves these inline (an OPAC public cover endpoint, a PDF viewer, an email attachment) and drops one of the two headers. It also means the per-resource allowlist provides no actual guarantee about what is on disk.
evidence: EXECUTED. `POST /t/probes1-x9/storage/covers` with an HTML body declared as `type=image/png` was accepted (201, ref covers/cmt5mnlskf8250764cdd8.png) and read back byte-identical as `<html><script>alert(1)</script></html>`. The same file declared honestly as text/html was correctly rejected 415. Also verified the good news: a filename of `../../../../tmp/pwn.png` had no effect — LocalDriver.put ignores originalname for the path and generates `covers/<cuid>.png`, and safeResolve() refuses any ref containing '..'.
fix: Add a magic-byte check in StorageService.put for the image resource types (the first 12 bytes distinguish JPEG/PNG/WebP/GIF unambiguously) and reject on mismatch with the declared type. Keep attachment + nosniff regardless.

title: The public /apply throttle fails open, and the only bot defence behind it is a honeypot field
what: RateLimitService.hit() fails closed only for keys starting with 'signup:'; every other bucket returns `{ allowed: true }` on a Redis error. The /apply bucket is keyed `apply:iph:<hash>`, so a Redis outage removes the form's only throttle entirely (the code comments this as intentional: 'Fails OPEN - a Redis outage must not eat leads'). The remaining bot defence is a single honeypot input named `website`. Each accepted submission writes a row to the control-plane applications table and enqueues an outbound notification email to the operator.
impact: During any Redis blip — or permanently, via finding 02's header rotation — the launch marketing form accepts unlimited submissions. Each one is a control-plane row plus an email to the operator's inbox, so the practical outcome is an inbox flood and a polluted lead table at the exact moment the Greek launch campaign is driving real traffic to that page. Trivially automated; the honeypot stops only naive scrapers.
evidence: READ: rate-limit.service.ts:78 `const failClosed = key.startsWith('signup:')` and :102 the catch branch returns `{ allowed: true, ... }` for everything else; applications.service.ts:112 keys the bucket `apply:iph:<sha256>`. EXECUTED (the header-rotation half): 8 submissions with rotating X-Real-IP all returned 303 and persisted, taking the applications table to 13 rows.
fix: Add a second bucket for /apply that is not IP-derived and fails closed — a global 'applications per hour' ceiling is fine here because, unlike signup, refusing a burst of applications for a few minutes is a far smaller harm than an unbounded flood. Given the campaign traffic, a Turnstile widget on the form is the cheaper real fix.

title: Password fields have a minimum length but no maximum
what: SignupDto.password and PasswordResetCompleteDto.newPassword are `@MinLength(12)` with no `@MaxLength`. Every other string field in these DTOs is bounded with @Length. LoginDto.password and CompleteSetupDto.newPassword are correctly bounded at 200.
impact: Small. The 100 KB body cap bounds the input and bcryptjs truncates at 72 bytes, so there is no hashing-cost amplification. The concrete harm is inconsistency: a user can set a 90 KB password at signup that LoginDto's `@Length(1, 200)` will then refuse at login, locking them out of the account they just created.
evidence: READ. signup.dto.ts:45-47 `@IsString() @MinLength(12, ...) password!: string;` with no @MaxLength; password-reset.dto.ts:21-22 the same for newPassword. Contrast login.dto.ts:22 `@Length(1, 200) password!: string;`.

title: No SQL injection found; the one $queryRawUnsafe is fully parameterized and every other raw query is a tagged template
what: Reviewed every raw-SQL site. help.service.ts:79 is the sole $queryRawUnsafe: the SQL string is a constant and all four values travel as $1..$4 bind parameters; the only value that reaches the query outside a bind is `config`, which is derived from a two-value locale allowlist (pickLocale), not from input. Everything else — storage.service.ts:76/188, members.service.ts:443, quota.service.ts:63, fleet.service.ts, loans/reservations/staff services, the jobs — uses Prisma tagged-template $executeRaw/$queryRaw, which binds. export-processors.ts:377 interpolates a table name into `SELECT * FROM "${name}"`, but that name comes from pg_tables of the database being exported, not from a request.
impact: None. Recorded so this dimension's negative result is on the record and does not have to be re-derived.
evidence: READ + EXECUTED. `grep -rn 'queryRaw|executeRaw' apps packages --include=*.ts` enumerated 13 non-test sites, all reviewed. Live probes returned clean results rather than errors or leakage: `GET /help/articles?q='); DROP TABLE users;--` -> 200 with `"query":"'); DROP TABLE users;--", "items":[]`; `GET /t/probes1-x9/catalog/books?after='";--` -> 200 empty page; `GET /t/probes1-x9/loans?status=../../etc/passwd` -> 400 with a proper allowlist message.
fix: None required. Keep $queryRawUnsafe out of the codebase or bind-parameterized if it must stay.

title: SSRF, CSV formula injection, zip bombs and body-size limits are all handled correctly
what: Four areas this dimension was asked to check came back clean, verified rather than assumed. (1) SSRF: the ISBN lookup is the only outbound call influenced by user input; the host is a hardcoded literal, the ISBN is reduced to digits and shape-checked before it reaches the URL, `redirect: 'manual'` stops a 3xx bounce to cloud metadata, there is a 5s AbortController timeout and a 1 MB streaming response cap. The other two fetch() sites (GitHub releases, Resend) take their URLs from env config, not from requests. (2) CSV formula injection: neutralizeFormula prefixes `'` to any cell starting with = + - @ TAB CR, and it is applied on all three CSV-producing paths — tenant/admin exports (cellValue), the public applications export (applications.controller.ts:139), and the import error report (import.service.ts:417). (3) xlsx decompression bombs: zip-guard.ts reads the ZIP central directory and rejects on declared expansion over 512 MB before exceljs inflates anything, with ZIP64 treated as too big. (4) Request bodies are capped and the cap returns a clean 413, not a 500. Path traversal in stored filenames is also handled — see finding 09's evidence.
impact: None. Recorded so these do not get re-audited.
evidence: READ for the code paths above. EXECUTED: a 3 MB JSON body returned `413 {"message":"That was too large to accept. Please use a smaller file or shorter text."}`; a multipart request with 20,000 text fields returned a clean 400 and the server stayed healthy; `GET /t/probes1-x9/catalog/isbn-lookup/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc` returned 404 with the friendly message (digitsOnly + isValidIsbnShape rejected it before any fetch).
